title: Ole Miss student apologizes and withdraws after racist doorbell video; family says it received death threats
excerpt: Alaina Kunes, 18, apologized and withdrew from the University of Mississippi after a viral doorbell video showed her making monkey gestures outside the apartment of three Black students. She says her family has since received death threats.
content:
🌎 BEYOND THE 956

A University of Mississippi student has apologized and withdrawn from the school after a viral doorbell-camera video showed her making monkey gestures outside the apartment of three Black students. She says she and her family have since received death threats and harassment.

The 13-second video, recorded by a Ring doorbell camera at about 8:37 p.m. on Friday, November 6, shows Alaina Kunes, 18, and another student thumping their chests and making monkey noises and gestures as they pass the apartment door. A third woman walking with them does not make any gestures or noises. The apartment is home to freshmen Jakiyra Metcalf, Kaiyden Caldwell and Victoria Johnson, who are Black.

Metcalf posted the video to TikTok on November 7. It has been viewed more than 12 million times.

University of Mississippi Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs Shawnboda Mead issued a letter on Sunday, November 8, condemning what she described as racist gestures directed toward other students. The university is investigating the incident.

On Tuesday, November 10, Kunes issued a statement through her attorney, Thomas G. Gardiner. “To the women I offended and to the Ole Miss community, I sincerely apologize,” she said. “Before the incident on November 6, I never met the women involved and was unaware of their race; however, I recognize my actions were insensitive, inappropriate, and deeply harmful. I have apologized to the women, and I pray they will forgive me.”

Gardiner confirmed that Kunes has withdrawn from the university, where she was a freshman. The university confirmed on November 10 that she is no longer a student.

In her statement, Kunes said she and her family have received death threats and harassment since the video spread online, and she thanked authorities for working to ensure their safety. On November 12, TMZ posted a voicemail it described as a death threat against Kunes and her family. The voicemail’s authenticity has not been independently confirmed.

Metcalf, Caldwell and Johnson appeared on CBS Mornings on November 11 to discuss the incident.

Sources: USA Today; Clarion Ledger; CBS News; TMZ.
